selected_title: An attained eventual reality threshold for a growing quartic arithmetic transform
editorial_decision: One sustained global paper should combine saddle estimates, exact arithmetic obstruction, polynomial approximation, attainment, confinement and collision. Do not split the easy endpoint topology into a purported complete proof of the global theorem.

definitions.transform: H_t(z)=integral_0^infinity exp(t*u^4)*K(u)*cos(u*z) du; t is real, z is complex. Growing positive quartic tilt, not exp(-t*u^4).
definitions.approximation: LP(t) means a sequence of real polynomials splitting over R converges to H_t locally uniformly on the whole complex plane.
definitions.starts: S={T in R: for every t>=T, LP(t)}; A=inf S. S is a set of eventual starting times, not by definition the set {t:LP(t)}.

exact_verified_scope: S is nonempty, A is finite and A>8; S=[A,infinity).
For every t>=A, all complex zeros of the actual H_t are real and LP(t) holds.
There is a nonreal zero for every t in some open neighborhood of 8.
For every epsilon>0 there is some s in (A-epsilon,A) and a nonreal zero of H_s.
A single finite B confines every nonreal zero for every t>=1.
There are s_n<A tending to A and nonreal zeros z_n tending to a real threshold zero.
At A there is a positive real zero of finite analytic multiplicity at least two.
For every sufficiently large t, every zero is real and simple. This is not endpoint simplicity.
prohibited_strengthenings: Do not assert {t: all zeros of H_t are real}=[A,infinity); earlier isolated reality times or intervals have not been excluded by the eventual-start statement.
Do not assert that every t<A has a nonreal zero, that all t>A have only simple zeros, or that the endpoint multiplicity is exactly two.
Do not assert a continuously tracked zero trajectory, first-exit/reentry history, numerical upper threshold or RH implication.
Do not replace a common stationary center in bounded and far regions by unrelated fixed-time limits.
Do not treat fixed-frequency cosine approximation, model-saddle existence or a certificate for a truncated kernel as the actual whole-plane theorem.

Attainment from compact-time continuity: For s_n tending to t with LP(s_n), choose for each n one real split polynomial Q_n approximating H_{s_n} within 1/(n+1) on |z|<=n. This is possible by local uniform polynomial convergence at that fixed time.

On every fixed compact K, eventually K is inside |z|<=n. Compact-uniform continuity in time gives sup_K|H_{s_n}-H_t| tending to zero. The triangle inequality proves Q_n tends locally uniformly to H_t; hence LP(t).

For each t>A, infimum approximation gives T in S with T<t, so LP(t). Apply the preceding diagonal argument to t_n=A+1/(n+1) to get LP(A). Thus A is in S, and the infimum and upward-closed definition give S=[A,infinity).
Nonreal zeros immediately below the endp: Fix epsilon>0 and T=A-epsilon/2. Since T is not in S, some t>=T fails LP(t). Since every t>=A satisfies LP(t), this chosen t is less than A.
The exact equivalence LP(t) iff all zeros of H_t are real then supplies a nonreal zero. This proves existence at some time in (A-epsilon,A), not at every earlier time.
Confinement and compactness: Choose a late time T0 after which all zeros are real. The bounded-time far-zero theorem provides a single radius B valid for 1<=t<=T0. Any nonreal zero at time t>=1 is either in that bounded-time disk or contradicts late-time reality. Thus one B works for all t>=1.
Choose s_n in (A-1/(n+1),A) with nonreal zero z_n. Since A>8, all these times are >=1. The common B puts z_n in a compact disk; select a convergent subsequence.
Joint continuity gives H_A(w)=0 at its limit, and threshold reality gives Im(w)=0. No escape to infinity or unproved path tracking is used.
The collision derivative: Suppose c=H_A prime(w) is nonzero. Joint continuity of the derivative gives a convex disk around the real w and a time neighborhood on which |H_s prime(q)-c|<=|c|/2.
For z,zbar in that disk, integrate the derivative along their segment. The triangle inequality applied after subtracting c(z-zbar) gives |H_s(z)-H_s(zbar)| >= |c|*|z-zbar|/2.
For the convergent nonreal zeros, conjugation symmetry makes both z_n and zbar_n zeros. They are distinct, contradicting this lower bound. Hence H_A prime(w)=0.

H_A(0)>0 excludes w=0. Evenness reflects a negative real w to a positive zero, with the derivative reflected oddly. The entire H_A is nonzero, so the order at that zero is finite and at least two. Exact double multiplicity does not follow.
Common-center whole-plane assembly: Let B(u)=4*pi*exp(4u). Choose M=2*exp(64) and R=max(N,120021), where N is the uniform far theorem cutoff in the stationary-center parameter.
For all sufficiently late t the bounded-ratio theorem supplies one actual real stationary center u>=R such that every zero in |z|<=M*B(u) is real and simple.

For the complementary region |z|>=2*exp(64)*B(u), the uniform far theorem applies to this same u and t. The regions cover the whole plane. Far real-zero simplicity is then added with the same cutoff and even reflection for negative real frequencies.
This is a valid assembly only after both actual uniform analytic theorems have full proofs; it is not a replacement for those analytic proofs.
Balanced amplitude identity: Given a nonzero complex center amplitude a and an analytic primitive P with fixed center value zero, let Pstar(z)=conj(P(conj(z))). Define E(z)=|a| exp((P(z)+Pstar(z))/2) and Phi(z)=arg(a)+(P(z)-Pstar(z))/(2i).
Then (a exp(P(z))+conj(a) exp(Pstar(z)))/2=E(z) cos(Phi(z)), and the sum of the two amplitude norms is 2|E(z)| cosh(Im(Phi(z))).
These exact identities convert relative pair-integral error into the weighted cosine error used in the local zero lemma. The argument of a is fixed; no varying principal argument is differentiated.
Buffered cosine perturbation lemma: Statement: let a be real and f holomorphic on a neighborhood of the closed disk |q-a|<=1, with f(conj q)=conj f(q), and |f(q)-cos(q)|<=delta=1/1000 on that disk. Every zero q0 with |q0-a|<=delta is real and simple.

At such a zero, |cos(q0)|<=delta. Since |sin(q)|<=exp(|Im q|)<3 throughout the unit disk, integration along the segment from a to q0 gives |cos(a)|<=delta+3*delta=1/250. The real identity sin(a)^2+cos(a)^2=1 then gives |sin(a)|>=1/2.

Set c=-sin(a). For |q-a|<=delta the circle |v-q|=1/2 remains inside the unit disk. Apply the Cauchy derivative estimate to h=f-cos, whose modulus is at most delta: |f prime(q)+sin(q)|<=2*delta. The same sine derivative bound gives |sin(q)-sin(a)|<=3*delta. Therefore |f prime(q)-c|<=5*delta<=|c|/2.
The small disk is convex. Integration of f prime-c along the segment between v and w gives |f(v)-f(w)-c(v-w)|<=|c|*|v-w|/2. Hence |f(v)-f(w)|>=|c|*|v-w|/2.

Both q0 and conj(q0) lie in that disk and are zeros, so the lower bound forces equality q0=conj(q0). Also |f prime(q0)|>=|c|/2>0. This proves exact reality and simplicity without claiming merely that the zero is near a cosine zero.
Phase straightening with the exact buffe: Inputs: g is entire and conjugation compatible; x is real; r,s>0, D>=0, D/s<=epsilon=10^-6 and 1/s<=r/2. E and Phi are analytic on |z-x|<r, E is nonzero, and both are conjugation compatible there. Assume |Phi prime(z)-s|<=D and |g(z)/E(z)-cos(Phi(z))|<=epsilon*cosh(Im(Phi(z))) throughout the disk. The source states global nonvanishing and conjugacy for E,Phi; those stronger hypotheses certainly give the local properties used here.

Take a zero z with |z-x|<r/2. Write p=Re(z), a=Phi(p), which is real by conjugacy. Define L(q)=p+(q-a)/s and f(q)=g(L(q))/E(L(q)). The closed disk |q-a|<=1 maps into |w-x|<r, because |p-x|<r/2 and |L(q)-p|<=1/s<=r/2. Thus f is holomorphic there and respects conjugation.

Integration of Phi prime-s from p to L(q) gives |Phi(L(q))-q|<=D/s<=epsilon. In particular Phi(L(q)) lies in |w-a|<2, hence |Im(Phi(L(q)))|<=2. On that disk |sin(w)|<=exp(2)<9 and cosh(Im(w))<=exp(2)<9. Therefore |f(q)-cos(q)|<=9*epsilon+9*epsilon=18*epsilon<1/1000.

At the original zero, the weighted error gives |cos(Phi(z))|<=epsilon*cosh(Im(Phi(z))). For w=u+iv, |cos(w)|^2=cos(u)^2+sinh(v)^2. Thus |tanh(v)|<=epsilon, so |v|<=arctanh(epsilon)<=epsilon/(1-epsilon)<=2*epsilon.

The vertical segment from p to z stays in the original disk. Since Re(Phi prime)>=s-D>=s/2 and Phi(p) is real, the real fundamental theorem along this segment gives |Im(Phi(z))|>=s*|Im(z)|/2. Hence s*|Im(z)|<=4*epsilon.
Set q0=a+s*(z-p). Then L(q0)=z, f(q0)=0 and |q0-a|=s*|Im(z)|<=4*epsilon<1/1000. The preceding buffered cosine lemma applies. Its conclusion Im(q0)=0 gives Im(z)=0, and f prime(q0) is nonzero.

At this zero, differentiating the quotient and the affine change of variables gives f prime(q0)=g prime(z)/(s*E(z)). Since s and E(z) are nonzero, g prime(z) is nonzero. These steps reconstruct the exact local reality/simple-zero mechanism used in the bounded-transition assembly.
Actual unequal-height contour pairing, c: Write F_z(w)=exp(t*w^4+i*z*w)*K_complex(w), J(z)=integral_0^infinity F_z(u) du and I_h(z)=integral_0^infinity F_z(u+i*h) du. The source proves for each real h with |h|<pi/8 that J(z)=I_h(z)+i*integral_0^h F_z(i*y)dy. That actual contour shift and its infinite-edge bounds remain separate analytic prerequisites.

Apply the shift at height h to J(z), and at height -k to J(-z). Evenness K_complex(-w)=K_complex(w) in the theta strip gives F_{-z}(-i*y)=F_z(i*y), so changing y to -y makes the second vertical contribution minus i*integral_0^k F_z(i*y)dy.
Conjugation gives I_{-k}(-z)=conj(I_k(conj(z))). Adding the two shifted integrals and dividing by two therefore gives H_t(z)=[I_h(z)+conj(I_k(conj(z)))+i*integral_k^h F_z(i*y)dy]/2.

When h=k the vertical contribution cancels. Independently corrected saddles generally give h unequal to k, so retaining the oriented interval integral from k to h is necessary. Approximate equality of heights is insufficient for deleting this term; it needs a quantitative relative error bound.
Complex Gaussian normalization and scala: For a complex b with Re(b)>0, the absolutely convergent Gaussian integral G(b)=integral_R exp(-b*s^2)ds equals sqrt(pi)/sqrt(b), with the analytic square-root branch in the right half-plane. One proof differentiates its absolutely dominated integral to obtain G prime=-G/(2b), so sqrt(b)*G is constant on that half-plane; its value on positive real b is the ordinary real Gaussian value. Thus |G|^2=pi/|b|. This standard calculation does not require Re(b) comparable to |b|.

For r>0, integration by parts on [r,R], using the derivative of exp(-b*s^2), gives integral_r^infinity exp(-b*s^2)ds=exp(-b*r^2)/(2*b*r)-(1/(2*b))*integral_r^infinity exp(-b*s^2)/s^2 ds. Taking absolute values and using Re(b)>0 gives at most 1/(|b|*r). Both tails together are at most 2/(|b|*r).

Under the exact far-saddle hypotheses, the source bounds x<=|b|<=4*x and Re(b)>0, so |G|>=1/(2*sqrt(x)). Its local comparison yields normalized error at most 2*sqrt(x)*[16*eta*r^2+8192*x*r^4+2/(x*r)], where eta=30005*exp(-4*Re(w)+4)<=10^8/x. The model-to-actual and cubic Taylor bounds entering that comparison are still to be reconstructed; this block does not assume they have been proved in the human exposition.

Set r=x^(-7/16). The three normalized terms are bounded respectively by 32*10^8*x^(-11/8), 16384*x^(-1/4), and 4*x^(-1/16), all tending to zero. The local smallness condition eta*r+2048*x*r^3<=1 eventually follows from eta*r<=10^8*x^(-23/16) and x*r^3=x^(-5/16). Also r<1/16 eventually.

This explains the chosen exponent 7/16 and why an oscillatory Gaussian tail bound in terms of |b| matters. It controls the full model Gaussian tails, not yet the complementary actual horizontal contour pieces.
Actual arithmetic kernel, entire flow an: For u>=0 every kernel summand factors as pi*n^2*exp(5*u)*(2*pi*n^2*exp(4*u)-3)*exp(-pi*n^2*exp(4*u)), n>=1. It is strictly positive since pi>3, n>=1 and exp(4*u)>=1. The Gaussian sums converge locally uniformly, so K is continuous and strictly positive on the half-line.

For v>=1 and n>=1, n^2*v>=(n^2+v)/2. Thus n^m exp(-pi*n^2*v) <= n^m exp(-pi*n^2/2)*exp(-pi*v/2). The sum of the first factor is finite. Applying this to the two theta moments gives K(u)<=C exp(9*u-pi*exp(4*u)/2) for u>=0 with one positive constant C.

For fixed k>=0 and real T,B, exponential growth dominates the quartic and linear polynomials: eventually T*u^4+(B+11)*u <= pi*exp(4*u)/2 and u^k<=exp(u). Consequently u^k exp(T*u^4+B*u)*K(u)<=C exp(-u) eventually. Continuity supplies integrability on compact initial intervals. Hence every polynomial moment with every real quartic/linear tilt is integrable.

On a compact set of (t,z), the absolute value of the kth spatial derivative of the exponential integrand is bounded by u^k exp(T*u^4+B*u)*K(u). Differentiation under the integral is therefore valid at every order. H_t is entire, even in z and conjugation compatible. H_t(0)>0 is an integral of a strictly positive function. The same dominated argument gives joint continuity of H_t and its spatial derivative in (t,z).

Joint continuity on [t0-1,t0+1] times a compact complex set is uniform continuity. It gives sup_{z in K}|H_t(z)-H_t0(z)| tending to zero as t tends to t0. This is the compact-time input in the endpoint diagonal argument.
Subquadratic actual growth: Set R=|z|. For u>=0, R*u<=u^3+R*sqrt(R): if u<=sqrt(R), use R*u<=R*sqrt(R); otherwise R<=u^2 and R*u<=u^3. Also u^3<=u^4+1, by splitting at u=1.

Therefore exp(t*u^4+R*u)*K(u)<=exp(1+R^(3/2))*exp((t+1)*u^4)*K(u). Since |cos(u*z)|<=exp(R*u), integration yields |H_t(z)|<=C_t exp(|z|^(3/2)), where C_t=exp(1)*integral_0^infinity exp((t+1)*u^4)*K(u)du is finite and positive. This checks the actual exponent strictly below two, not an assumed order estimate.
Even finite-disk factorization and real: Statement used: let f be entire and even, with f(0) real and nonzero, and |f(z)|<=C exp(|z|^(3/2)). If all its zeros are real, then f is a locally uniform limit on C of real split polynomials. Apply this statement to the actual H_t using the preceding block. The argument below is a classical finite-disk reconstruction; no unverified classification premise is introduced.

Choose R tending to infinity through radii having no zeros on the circle. There are only countably many forbidden radii because the nonzero entire function has isolated zeros. List all zeros a inside |z|<R with multiplicity, and set B_R(z)=product_a [R*(z-a)/(R^2-conj(a)*z)]. Each denominator is nonzero on the closed disk. Each factor has modulus one on its boundary, and modulus |a|/R at zero. No zero a equals zero.

The quotient h_R=f/B_R extends across all the finitely many zeros to a holomorphic zero-free function on the disk and a neighborhood of its boundary. The maximum modulus principle and the unit boundary modulus give |h_R(z)|<=M_f(R)<=C exp(R^(3/2)) inside. Since |B_R(0)|<=1, one has |h_R(0)|>=|f(0)|.

The zero multiset is invariant under a mapping to -a, with equal multiplicities. The pair of Blaschke factors for a and -a is even, so B_R and h_R are even. On the simply connected disk choose the analytic logarithm g_R with exp(g_R)=h_R/h_R(0) and g_R(0)=0. Uniqueness of the normalized logarithm implies g_R is even. Its real part is at most log(C/|f(0)|)+R^(3/2), hence at most a positive A_R=O(1+R^(3/2)).

For completeness the logarithm estimate needs no unstated factorization theorem: define v_R=g_R/(2*A_R-g_R). The denominator has strictly positive real part, and |2*A_R-g_R|^2-|g_R|^2=4*A_R*(A_R-Re(g_R))>=0. Thus |v_R|<=1 on the disk. It is even and vanishes at zero, so the Schwarz lemma with its double zero gives |v_R(z)|<=(|z|/R)^2. Solving g_R=2*A_R*v_R/(1+v_R) yields |g_R(z)|<=2*A_R*(|z|/R)^2/(1-(|z|/R)^2). This tends to zero uniformly on each fixed compact set as R tends to infinity. Hence h_R/h_R(0) tends locally uniformly to one.

To control the denominator product, first bound zero counts. Choose a zero-free boundary radius rho in (2R,3R). The zero-free h_rho has harmonic log modulus, so its value at zero is the boundary mean of log|h_rho|, which is the boundary mean of log|f| and is at most log M_f(rho). Since f(0)=B_rho(0)*h_rho(0), this gives sum_{|a|<rho} log(rho/|a|)<=log M_f(rho)-log|f(0)|. Every zero inside radius R contributes at least log(2). Thus n_f(R)<=O(1+R^(3/2)). This is the finite-disk Jensen estimate with its derivation stated explicitly.

Normalize the finite product: B_R(z)/B_R(0)=N_R(z)/D_R(z), where N_R=product_a(1-z/a), D_R=product_a(1-conj(a)*z/R^2). Pairing the zeros a,-a gives D_R=product_pairs(1-conj(a)^2*z^2/R^4). On |z|<=r, the sum of the absolute pair corrections is at most n_f(R)*r^2/(2*R^2)=O_r(R^(-1/2)). The elementary finite-product bound |product(1-w_j)-1|<=exp(sum|w_j|)-1 shows D_R tends locally uniformly to one.

The exact identity f/f(0)=[B_R/B_R(0)]*[h_R/h_R(0)] and convergence of the last factor to one now give B_R/B_R(0) tending locally uniformly to f/f(0). Multiply by D_R to obtain N_R tending to f/f(0). Every zero a is real by hypothesis, so f(0)*N_R is a real polynomial splitting over R, with the exact normalization restored. This proves the required approximation.
Reverse implication by vertical modulus,: For a real root r, the modulus |x+i*y-r|=sqrt((x-r)^2+y^2) is nondecreasing in |y|. Taking finite products gives |P(x+i*a)|<=|P(x+i*b)| whenever a^2<=b^2 for every real split polynomial P (the zero polynomial is harmless).

The inequality survives pointwise limits of a locally uniformly convergent polynomial sequence. If a nonzero entire limit f vanished at x+i*y with y nonzero, it would vanish at every x+i*v with |v|<=|y|. In particular it would have zeros x+i*y/(n+1) accumulating at x. The identity theorem would force f identically zero, a contradiction.

Thus every zero of a nonzero entire split-polynomial limit is real. Together with the finite-disk argument this gives exactly LP(t) iff all actual H_t zeros are real, using the actual growth, evenness and nonzero origin rather than a blanket converse to a zero-limit principle.
Elementary four-term and cutoff error bo: These human bounds reorganize the same verified error targets; they are not newly added Lean declarations. Let a=8/5 and k=0,1,2. On 0<=u<=a, u^k<=3. Since exp(4u)>=1+4u+(4u)^4/24, one has 3*n^2*(exp(4u)-1)>=12*n^2*u+32*n^2*u^4>=9u+8u^4 for n>=1.

The positive omitted theta terms n>=5 are bounded above by 32*n^4*exp(9u-3*n^2*exp(4u)), using pi<4 and pi>3. After multiplying by u^k*exp(8u^4), their total is at most 96*sum_{n>=5} n^4*exp(-3*n^2). The exponential series gives n^4<=2*exp(n^2), so this is at most 192*sum_{n>=5}exp(-2*n^2).

Write n=5+j: 2*n^2>=50+20j. The geometric sum is less than 2*exp(-50). The final bound is 384*exp(-50)<384*(2/5)^50<10^-17, since exp(1)>5/2 (already the first four Taylor terms exceed 5/2). This proves the whole four-term weighted remainder bound used on the finite integration interval.

For the full-kernel cutoff, the earlier envelope constant can be bounded explicitly by 176. Indeed theta_m(1/2)<=sum n^4*exp(-(3/2)*n^2)<=2*sum exp(-n^2/2)<=2/(exp(1/2)-1)<=4 for m=2,4. Here n^m<=n^4, n^4<=2*exp(n^2), n^2>=n and exp(1/2)>=3/2. Thus C<=2*16*4+3*4*4=176 in K(u)<=C exp(9u-(pi/2)*exp(4u)).

For u>=a, the functions u^4*exp(-4u) and u*exp(-4u) decrease because their derivatives have factors 1-u and 1-4u. The rational inequality 8*a^4+111*a < (3/2)*(5/2)^6, together with exp(4a)>exp(6)>(5/2)^6, implies 8u^4+111u <=(3/2)*exp(4u) for u>=a.

Since u^k<=exp(2u) for k<=2, the absolute full integrand tail is at most 176*exp(-100u) for u>=a. Its integral is at most (176/100)*exp(-160)<(176/100)*2^-160. Adding the finite-interval theta error a*10^-17 gives less than 10^-16. This proves the actual kth-derivative versus four-term finite integral error target, uniformly in real spatial frequency; cos and sin have modulus at most one.
Exact finite arithmetic and final Laguer: At x=632083/10000, set F_k(u)=exp(8u^4)*K_4(u)*c_k(u), with c_0=cos(xu), c_1=-u*sin(xu), c_2=-u^2*cos(xu). Partition [0,8/5] into 160 intervals [j/100,(j+1)/100], center c_j=(2j+1)/200 and half-width h=1/200.

On each cell take the degree-15 Taylor polynomial of F_k about c_j. Odd powers integrate to zero; the exact polynomial integral is sum_{i=0}^7 [F_k^(2i)(c_j)/(2i)!]*[2*h^(2i+1)/(2i+1)]. If the normalized sixteenth derivative is at most 10^22 throughout the cell, Taylor with integral remainder gives cell integral error <=2*10^22*h^17/17<10^-16. Summing 160 cells gives total polynomial-quadrature error <=16/10^15. With the actual-tail bound above, every actual derivative differs from its total polynomial by <=161/10^16.

The finite certificate uses outward rounded dyadic intervals with denominator scale 2^192. Addition, multiplication, rational division and finite convolution retain interval membership. For exp(x), divide the argument by 2^s until its magnitude is at most one, enclose the first 48 Taylor terms with remainder +/-2/48!, and square s times. The actual source uses s=4 for exp(4u) and s=16 for the exponential phases. Trigonometric centers are range reduced by 2^8, enclosed by their 48-term real/imaginary exponential series, and doubled eight times. Whole-cell trigonometric values may use the enclosure [-1,1].

Normalized derivative coefficients propagate by finite convolution for products. For an exponential exp(phi), if A_j=phi^(j)/j! and B_j=(exp(phi))^(j)/j!, the exact identity is B_0=exp(phi) and B_n=(1/n)*sum_{j=1}^n j*A_j*B_{n-j}. The two phases are phi_{n,b}(u)=8u^4+b*u-pi*n^2*exp(4u), b=9,5 and n=1,...,4, retaining their distinct constants. Monomial and sine/cosine coefficients supply the three channels.

The existing frozen Lean certificate proves all 160 whole-cell sixteenth-coefficient checks and all 480 centered even-polynomial interval inclusions by exact kernel reduction. Their archived endpoint integers are included in the certificate_transcription field, at common denominator 10^22. This editorial calculation independently re-sums those integers and checks the final rational margin; it does not claim to rerun the interval engine or replace the baseline Lean audit.

The exact lower/upper endpoint numerator sums for channels 0,1,2 are respectively [-1641482419995,-1641482419749], [3656317813,3656318043], [-1460002952576,-1460002952347]. Divide them by 10^22, then enlarge by 161/10^16 for the actual derivatives. The enlarged channel-0 and channel-2 upper endpoints are negative; let their negatives be b0,b2>0 and let b1 be the enlarged absolute channel-1 bound. Then H_8 prime(x)^2-H_8(x)*H_8 doubleprime(x)<=b1^2-b0*b2<-2/10^20 by exact rational arithmetic.

For a real split polynomial P, P prime(x)^2-P(x)*P doubleprime(x)>=0 at every real x: away from its roots divide by P(x)^2 and obtain the sum over real roots of their multiplicities/(x-root)^2; at a root extend by continuity. Locally uniform entire convergence gives convergence of the first two derivatives by the Cauchy formula. Hence the same inequality holds for an entire split-polynomial limit.

The strictly negative actual H_8 expression excludes LP(8). Continuity in t of the three actual derivatives at this fixed x preserves strict negativity on an open neighborhood of 8. The all-real/split-polynomial equivalence then supplies a nonreal actual zero at every time in that neighborhood. Because the neighborhood includes some times greater than 8, every eventual start lies above a fixed 8+delta; consequently A>8 once nonemptiness has been proved by the separate global saddle theorem.

theorem exists_actual_product_approximation (t : ℝ) :
    ∃ r : ℝ → ℝ, ∃ h : ℝ → ℂ → ℂ,
      (∀ R : ℝ, 1 ≤ R → 2*R < r R ∧ r R < 2*R+1 ∧
        ECanonicalDecomp (flow t) (h R) (r R) ∧
        divisor (flow t) (sphere 0 (r R)) = 0 ∧
        inverseZeroProduct t (r R) 0 ≠ 0 ∧
        ∀ z ∈ closedBall (0 : ℂ) (r R),
          flow t z = inverseZeroProduct t (r R) z * h R z) ∧
      TendstoLocallyUniformly
        (fun R z => inverseZeroProduct t (r R) z / inverseZeroProduct t (r R) 0)
        (fun z => flow t z / flow t 0) atTop ∧
      TendstoLocallyUniformly
        (fun R z => flow t 0 * (inverseZeroProduct t (r R) z / inverseZeroProduct t (r R) 0))
        (flow t) atTop
